abstract: Abstract Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using sunlight offers a route to renewable fuel, but translating this reaction into systems suitable for industrial implementation remains difficult. Photocatalyst sheets can overcome key limitations of common direct water-splitting approaches (photoelectrochemical devices and photocatalyst dispersions), but existing photocatalyst sheets rely on inorganic semiconductor nanoparticles and processing techniques that can be difficult to scale. Here we show that solution-processed organic semiconductors can form water-splitting photocatalyst sheets by simply tailoring the charge extraction layer beneath the light-absorbing film. A single organic semiconductor active layer (deposited as a bulk heterojunction blend) drives either hydrogen or oxygen evolution depending on its underlying molecular contact, yielding photocathode and photoanode half-cells with well-matched photocurrents. Combining both reactions on one substrate using a microdomain-patterned molecular underlayer affords a photocatalyst sheet that achieves unassisted water splitting under simulated sunlight for over 2 h and generates hydrogen at a stabilized rate of 1.3 µmol h −1 cm −2 , which corresponds to a solar-to-hydrogen conversion efficiency of 0.1%.
hook: An all-organic sheet splits water under simulated sunlight, at 0.1% solar-to-hydrogen efficiency.
summary: One organic semiconductor blend makes hydrogen or oxygen depending on the molecular contact layer beneath it. Patterning both contacts on one substrate gave a sheet that split water unassisted at 1.3 micromoles of hydrogen per hour per square centimeter. Efficiency is low and operation was shown for only about 2 hours.
title: An organic semiconductor-based photocatalyst sheet for overall solar-driven water splitting
